name: Ken Saro-Wiwa

family_context_summary: Born into a ruling Ogoni family in Bori, Nigeria; father Chief Jim Wiwa was a forest ranger who held a title in the Nigerian chieftaincy system. The family enjoyed a marginally more privileged life than other Ogoni youth.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a chief in the Ogoni chieftaincy system and a forest ranger; no documented domain expertise in writing or activism transferred to Ken.
evidence_summary: Ken Saro-Wiwa was a distinguished student from a ruling Ogoni family who earned a scholarship to the University of Ibadan and graduated with honors in English around 1965. By age 26 he was teaching but had not yet achieved a material career milestone; his political appointments (1968-69) and literary output (from 1985) all came after age 26.

name: Tadej Pogačar
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 2020 Tour de France at age 21, becoming the second-youngest winner in the race's history and the first rider to win the general, mountains, and young rider classifications simultaneously; also won the Tour de l'Avenir in 2018 (age 19), the Tour of California in 2019 (age 20, youngest UCI WorldTour stage race winner), and three stages at the 2019 Vuelta a España.
early_history_summary: Pogačar grew up in the small town of Klanec, Komenda, Slovenia, and followed his older brother Tilen into cycling at age nine, joining the Rog Ljubljana club. At age 13 he was discovered by former Road World Championship medalist Andrej Hauptman, who noticed him about to lap a group of much older teenagers. He won the Tour de l'Avenir in 2018 riding for the Slovenian national team and signed with UAE Team Emirates for 2019.
primary_leverage_engine: Physical talent and all-round cycling ability
family_context_summary: Born to Mirko and Marjeta Pogačar in the small town of Komenda, Slovenia (population ~6,000). Parents were never cyclists and had limited knowledge of the sport. The family had modest means; his mother stated they 'never had much money and always had to watch every euro.' His older brother Tilen introduced him to cycling.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family background in cycling. Parents were not athletes and had little knowledge of the sport. Father worked on a family farm; mother raised the children. Older brother Tilen was the first to take up cycling, and Tadej followed.
evidence_summary: Pogačar started cycling at age nine following his older brother Tilen into the Rog Ljubljana club in a small Slovenian town. At 13, he was discovered by Andrej Hauptman when he was about to lap much older riders, showing exceptional natural ability. His parents had no cycling background and modest finances, but the Slovenian cycling ecosystem and Hauptman's mentorship provided a pathway. He won the Tour de l'Avenir at 19, signed with UAE Team Emirates, and won the Tour de France at 21 with a dramatic time trial performance. His physical talent and early, intense specialization in cycling were the dominant factors.
starting_point: Born to modest-income parents Mirko and Marjeta Pogačar in the small town of Klanec, Komenda, Slovenia (population ~6,000); father worked on a family farm, mother raised the children.
current_position: Rides for UAE Team Emirates XRG as UCI world No.1 cyclist; four-time Tour de France winner (2020, 2021, 2024, 2025); two-time World Road Race champion; widely considered one of the greatest cyclists of all time.

trajectory.event: Raced his first official cycling competition following older brother Tilen into the sport.
Won the Tour de l'Avenir, the premier under-23 stage race, riding for the Slovenian national team.
Won the Tour of California as the youngest UCI WorldTour stage race winner and took three stages at the Vuelta a España finishing third overall.
Won the Tour de France on his debut, becoming the second-youngest winner ever and the first rider to win general, mountains, and young rider classifications simultaneously.
Won his second Tour de France and scored his first Monument victories at Liège–Bastogne–Liège and Giro di Lombardia.
Completed the Giro d'Italia–Tour de France double and won the World Championship road race, achieving the Triple Crown of Cycling.
Won his fourth Tour de France and became the first rider to retain both the Tour de France and World Championship titles simultaneously.

name: Vladimir Kramnik
milestone_by_age_26: Defeated Garry Kasparov in 2000 to become the Classical World Chess Champion at age 25, winning the match 8.5–6.5 without losing a single game; also became the youngest ever world No.1 rated player in January 1996 at age 20, and won individual gold at the 1992 Chess Olympiad at age 17.
early_history_summary: Kramnik was born in Tuapse, a small town on the Black Sea, to a family of artists. He learned chess from his father at age five and quickly became regional champion. At age 11, his games were sent to Mikhail Botvinnik, who recognized his talent and invited him to the Botvinnik-Kasparov chess school. He won world U16 and U18 championships and became a grandmaster in 1991 at age 16. Kasparov insisted on his selection for the 1992 Russian Olympiad team despite his junior status.
family_context_summary: Born in Tuapse, a provincial industrial town on the Black Sea, in a family of artists. His biological father Boris Sokolov was a painter and sculptor; his mother Irina Fedorovna was a Ukrainian music teacher. He described his hometown as a normal working-class place where some classmates went to prison.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family background in chess. Father was a painter and sculptor; mother was a music teacher. Father taught him chess at age five but was not a chess professional. The family was working class in a provincial Soviet town.
evidence_summary: Kramnik learned chess at five from his artist father in a provincial Soviet town. At 11, a local chess enthusiast sent his games to Mikhail Botvinnik, who recognized his talent and invited him to the elite Botvinnik-Kasparov chess school. He won world U16 and U18 titles, became a grandmaster at 16, and was championed by Kasparov for the 1992 Olympiad team. He became world No.1 at 20 and defeated Kasparov for the world title at 25 without losing a game. The Botvinnik school, Kasparov's mentorship, and his innate prodigy-level talent were the dominant early advantages.
starting_point: Born in the provincial industrial town of Tuapse on the Black Sea, Soviet Union, to a painter/sculptor father and Ukrainian music teacher mother; working-class family of artists with no chess background.
current_position: Retired from professional chess in January 2019; former Classical World Chess Champion (2000–2006) and undisputed World Chess Champion (2006–2007); peak FIDE rating 2817.

trajectory.event: Became an international grandmaster after winning world U16 and U18 championships.
Won individual gold medal at the Chess Olympiad in Manila on Kasparov's insistence, scoring 8.5/9 with a 2958 performance rating.
Became the youngest ever world No.1 rated player, ending Kasparov's continuous reign since 1985.
Defeated Garry Kasparov 8.5–6.5 in London to become Classical World Chess Champion without losing a single game.
Defeated FIDE champion Veselin Topalov in a reunification match to become the first undisputed World Chess Champion since 1993.
Lost the world championship title to Viswanathan Anand at the World Chess Championship tournament in Mexico City.
Publicly announced retirement from professional classical chess to focus on chess education projects.

His 1958 thesis on telescopic meteors won first prize in a national competition. He then began doctoral research at the Astronomical Institute of the Czechoslovak Academy of Sciences under Professor Luboš Perek.
family_context_summary: Born in Zábřeh na Moravě, Czechoslovakia, to Hynek and Jarmila Kohoutek. Father was a high school teacher. His brother Ctirad Kohoutek was a Czech composer.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a high school teacher; brother was a composer. No documented family background in astronomy or sciences directly transferred to Luboš.
evidence_summary: Kohoutek was interested in astronomy from high school and studied physics and astronomy at Czech universities, winning a national first prize for his 1958 thesis on telescopic meteors. He began doctoral research at the Czechoslovak Academy of Sciences, but his major scientific contributions—the Catalogue of Galactic Planetary Nebulae (1967) and Comet Kohoutek (1973)—came after age 26. name: Louis Andriessen
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. His major works—De Volharding (1972), De Staat (1976)—and his founding of influential ensembles came in the 1970s.
early_history_summary: Born in Utrecht into a prominent musical family, the son of composer Hendrik Andriessen. He studied composition privately with his father from 1953-57, then at the Royal Conservatory of The Hague under Kees van Baaren (1957-62), graduating with a first prize. He then studied with Luciano Berio in Milan and Berlin (1962-65). Early compositions include Series for two pianos (1958) and Nocturnen (1959).
family_context_summary: Born into a prominent Dutch musical family in Utrecht. Father Hendrik Andriessen was a composer and professor of composition at the Royal Conservatory of The Hague, later its director. Brother Jurriaan Andriessen was also a composer, and uncle Willem Andriessen was a composer and pianist. The family tradition went back to his great-grandfather, a choir conductor and music teacher.
parent_family_domain_summary: Deep family-domain apprenticeship in music: father was a composer and composition professor, brother and uncle were composers, and the family tradition spanned four generations. Louis studied composition privately with his father from age 14.
evidence_summary: Andriessen was born into a four-generation musical dynasty: his father Hendrik was a composition professor at the Royal Conservatory of The Hague, his brother and uncle were composers, and he began studying composition with his father at 14. He graduated from the conservatory with a first prize in 1962 and studied with Luciano Berio. However, his major internationally recognized works and ensemble founding came in the 1970s, well after age 26.

name: Valentino

name: Pak Se-ri
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1998 U.S. Women's Open at age 20 in a dramatic 20-hole playoff, and the 1998 LPGA Championship, becoming LPGA Rookie of the Year and AP Female Athlete of the Year; also won the 2001 Women's British Open and 2002 LPGA Championship for four total majors by age 25, and won six tournaments on the KLPGA Tour in 1996-97 before joining the LPGA.
early_history_summary: Born in Taejon, South Korea, Pak was a track star before her father, a former professional baseball player, introduced her to golf at age 14. Her father designed an intense training regimen including pre-dawn stair running, 800 daily shot practices, and nighttime cemetery visits to build mental toughness. She won 30 amateur tournaments, turned professional in 1996, and dominated the Korean LPGA with six wins in 14 events before moving to the U.S. at age 20 to join the LPGA Tour.
family_context_summary: Born in Taejon, South Korea. Father Jun Chul Pak was a former professional baseball player who ran a construction materials business (which failed, leading to a brief emigration to Hawaii). He was a plus-handicap amateur golfer who became Pak's primary coach, designing an extreme training regimen. Mother's details not documented. Pak is the second of three daughters.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was a former professional baseball player and plus-handicap amateur golfer who personally coached Pak from age 14 with an extreme regimen including 5:30 AM stair runs, 800 daily shots, and nighttime cemetery visits. He transferred athletic training knowledge and golf fundamentals directly. Samsung also provided sponsorship support including access to David Leadbetter as coach.
evidence_summary: Pak Se-ri started golf at 14 (late for an elite golfer) but was transformed by her father's extreme training regimen—pre-dawn stair runs, 800 daily practice shots, nighttime cemetery visits for mental toughness. Her father, a former pro baseball player and plus-handicap golfer, was her primary coach. She won 30 amateur tournaments, dominated the KLPGA with six wins in 14 events, then moved alone to the U.S. at 20 without knowing English. In her 1998 LPGA rookie season she won two majors including the U.S. Women's Open, becoming AP Female Athlete of the Year and sparking the Korean women's golf wave. Samsung's sponsorship provided access to David Leadbetter as coach.
starting_point: Born in Taejon, South Korea, to a former professional baseball player father who ran a construction materials business (which later failed) and became her demanding golf coach; second of three daughters in a middle-class family.
current_position: Retired professional golfer (2016); World Golf Hall of Fame inductee (2007, youngest ever at age 29); 25 LPGA Tour wins including 5 major championships; resides in Orlando, Florida.

trajectory.event: Turned professional and won six of 14 tournaments on the Korean LPGA Tour, finishing second in seven others.
Won the U.S. Women's Open and LPGA Championship in her LPGA rookie season, earning Rookie of the Year and AP Female Athlete of the Year honors.

Won the LPGA Championship for her fourth major title.
Won her fifth major at the LPGA Championship, qualifying for the World Golf Hall of Fame as the youngest inductee ever.

name: Ruzena Bajcsy
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found. By 1959 (age 26), Bajcsy had earned her MS in electrical engineering from Slovak Technical University but was sent to work in an electronics factory for five years as an 'enemy of the state' after a student speech. Her PhD came in 1967 (age 34), her second PhD from Stanford in 1972, and her faculty position at Penn in 1972.
early_history_summary: Born Jewish in Bratislava, Czechoslovakia in 1933, Bajcsy was orphaned at age 11 when Nazi troops killed her parents. She and her sister were cared for by the Red Cross in orphanages and foster homes. Despite this, she excelled in school and enrolled at Slovak Technical University to study electrical engineering. After earning her MS, a student speech praising Czech educator Comenius over the Russian education system led to her being labeled an 'enemy of the state' and sent to work in an electronics factory for five years.
family_context_summary: Born Jewish in Bratislava, Czechoslovakia in 1933. Both parents were killed by Nazis when she was 11, leaving her and her sister as war orphans under Red Cross care. She moved between orphanages and foster parents but remained a strong student.
parent_family_domain_summary: Parents were killed by Nazis when she was 11; no documented family domain expertise in engineering or computing. Family's Jewish background and wartime orphaning shaped her early life profoundly.
evidence_summary: Bajcsy was orphaned at 11 by the Nazis and raised in orphanages and foster care in Czechoslovakia. She excelled academically and earned an MS in electrical engineering from Slovak Technical University, but was then forced to work in an electronics factory for five years as a political punishment. Her scientific career—PhD (1967), Stanford (1967-72), Penn faculty (1972), GRASP Lab founding (1978)—all came after age 26. No material career milestone occurred by age 26.

name: Trevor Berbick
milestone_by_age_26: Won the Canadian Heavyweight Championship on May 26, 1979 at age 24, and scored a major upset by knocking out former WBA heavyweight champion John Tate in June 1980 at age 25; also won a bronze medal at the 1975 Pan American Games and represented Jamaica at the 1976 Montreal Olympics before turning professional in September 1976.
early_history_summary: Born in Port Antonio, Portland Parish, Jamaica, Berbick first took up boxing at age 19 while working at the U.S. Naval Base at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba. Despite having only 11 amateur bouts, he won a bronze medal at the 1975 Pan American Games and represented Jamaica at the 1976 Olympics. After the Olympics he emigrated to Canada and turned professional in September 1976, winning his first 11 fights (10 by knockout) before winning the Canadian heavyweight title in May 1979.
family_context_summary: Born in the Norwich area of Port Antonio, Portland Parish, Jamaica. Family background and financial circumstances are not documented in reviewed sources. He worked at the Guantanamo Bay U.S. Naval Base as a young man before taking up boxing.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No family background in boxing or athletics recorded.
evidence_summary: Berbick started boxing at 19 while working at Guantanamo Bay Naval Base, with only 11 amateur bouts before winning Pan Am bronze and competing at the 1976 Olympics. He emigrated to Canada, turned pro, and won his first 11 fights before claiming the Canadian heavyweight title at 24. His physical attributes—over 6'2", broad and muscular—compensated for limited technical skill and experience. He had no documented family support, coaching pipeline, or financial backing, making his rise largely self-created through physical talent and determination.

current_position: Died on October 28, 2006, at age 52 in Port Antonio, Jamaica; murdered by his nephew. Final role: former WBC heavyweight champion (1986).
